title: Moderators of noise-induced cognitive change in healthy adults
research_question: To elucidate the possible moderators of both social and nonsocial noise-induced changes in cognitive performance in healthy adults.

participants.description: 54 healthy participants (24 men, 30 women) aged 18-64 years (Mean=38.20, SD=11.16), with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, fluent English, and no hearing impairment. Mean full scale IQ was 117.61 (SD=12.86). Exclusion criteria included IQ <80, organic brain disorder, substance abuse disorder, or schizophrenia spectrum disorder.
participants.recruitment: Recruited via King's College London circulars to staff and students, online posts on the East Dulwich forum and the Experimatch website, and the Unusual Experiences Inquiry Studies (UNIQUE) research register.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three noise conditions: 1) Quiet (~30 dB) in a sound-proofed laboratory. 2) Urban noise (building-site noise, no social elements). 3) Social noise (background babble with no distinguishable speech and footsteps from a crowded hall). Urban and social noise had a background level of 68 dB with louder peaks of 78 dB. Mean energy level (dBA Leq), time profile, and number/duration of peaks were matched across urban and social conditions.

mechanisms: Individuals with poorer baseline cognitive ability may display reduced noise-induced changes in cognitive performance due to having less room to reduce performance.
Individuals with lower baseline performance may counteract their lower cognitive reserves and the addition of stress by adopting a more effortful response strategy.
Individuals with lower cognitive reserves may adopt a strategy of focussing attention on the central aspect of the task, resulting in less noise-disruption or even facilitation.
Individuals with Cognitive Disorganization (CogDis) are purported to have lower attention capacity, and facilitation under social noise could be representative of a more effortful response style.
moderators: Schizotypy (Unusual Experiences, Cognitive Disorganization, Introverted Anhedonia, Impulsive Nonconformity)
implementation_implications: The identified moderators (paranoia, sleep disturbances, noise sensitivity, cognitive disorganization) should be considered in studies aiming to reduce the detrimental effects of occupational and residential noise.
It is important to study noise effects in clinical populations characterized by high levels of paranoia, sleep disturbances, noise sensitivity, and cognitive disorganization.

limitations: Possible fatigue or habituation to noise in tasks at the end of the cognitive battery.
The range of some individual difference variables (e.g., paranoia, stress, anxiety) was not representative of higher scores, as expected in healthy samples.
Individual difference variables were assessed on one occasion and may have fluctuated for sleep quality or state-dependent variables (e.g., depression, anxiety, stress).
